idiom_name: capability by construction (ownership, no ambient handles) plus CommandExt uid/gid/groups for children
implementation_notes: Rust makes the capability idea structural in-process: a function can only do what the values it is given permit, ownership cannot be duplicated by accident, and there is no ambient global handle to the filesystem or the network - the capability is the handle itself, and the type system keeps it from being aliased away, which is as close as a mainstream language comes to making the least-authority rule hard to bypass. For processes, std exposes the credentials directly: CommandExt::uid and gid set the child's identity, setting uid also triggers setgroups(0, NULL) when no groups were specified so that supplementary groups cannot hand the child permissions nobody granted, CommandExt::groups sets them explicitly, and OpenOptionsExt::mode controls the permissions of created files. Where a job needs a kernel privilege instead of a uid, ecosystem crates wrap Linux capabilities and seccomp or Landlock around that syscall surface. The classic rights-table form is still justified when authority is runtime data - a multi-tenant service deciding per request - because the type-level version cannot model rights that change while the program runs.
pitfalls: Ownership is not a sandbox: unsafe blocks, transmute, and dependencies that open what they like can step outside the type discipline, so isolate untrusted code in a process or a sandboxed crate rather than relying on types alone.

uid() does not cover every grant: the documentation notes that it triggers setgroups(0, NULL) only when no groups were specified, so a stale supplementary group list - or credentials filled in from configuration - can still hand the child rights nobody intended.

pre_exec runs between fork and exec, where only async-signal-safe work is allowed and even allocating an error may fail; a drop or policy check placed there can deadlock rather than enforce, so prefer the typed CommandExt knobs.
